chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Long-Term Debt Cycle in India

lessons.title: Does India Have a Long-Term Debt Cycle? Bank Credit, Household Debt, and Corporate Leverage

body.text: India does not show the mature long-term debt cycle signature this course has spent four chapters building. Its combined government, household, and corporate debt is moderate by global standards, and growth is still driven more by Chapter 1's Force One, productivity and demographics, than by an ageing, over-leveraged credit cycle. That does not mean there is nothing to watch.

children.text: Chapter 2's Lesson 1 promised that India's position would be read from balance sheet data rather than from a multi-decade policy rate history, since the RBI's formal inflation-targeting framework only dates to 2016. This lesson delivers on that promise, walking through India's three main debt stocks, government, household, and corporate, in turn, before Lesson 2 covers the 2018 IL&FS shock and the broader bank NPA crisis in full, and Lesson 3 pulls everything into a single current read.
Government Debt-to-GDP: Elevated by Covid, on a Declining Path Since

markDefs.definition: The total debt of India's central and state governments combined, expressed as a percentage of GDP, the measure commonly used by the IMF and RBI for cross-country comparison.

children.text: ratio rose sharply during the Covid-19 pandemic, reaching close to 90% of GDP at its peak, as tax revenue fell and emergency spending rose. It has eased gradually since, back toward the low-to-mid 80s as a percentage of GDP, helped by the government's stated fiscal glide path targeting a lower central fiscal deficit over subsequent years and by nominal GDP growth doing genuine work on the denominator, exactly the r-versus-g mechanism from Chapter 3's Lesson 3. This is elevated relative to India's own pre-pandemic levels, but remains well below the government debt levels seen in Chapter 4's Japan case, and is trending down rather than up.
Household Debt-to-GDP: Low by Global Standards, Fastest-Growing of the Three

India's household debt-to-GDP ratio is low relative to most large economies, commonly cited at roughly 40% of GDP in recent years, up meaningfully from around 30% less than a decade earlier. The pace of that increase, not just its level, is what deserves attention: unsecured retail lending, personal loans and credit cards in particular, grew rapidly enough that the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit exposures for banks and NBFCs in November 2023, a direct, real-world example of a regulator leaning against Chapter 1's Lesson 2 collateral-and-borrowing feedback loop before it went further. More recently, asset quality stress has emerged specifically in the microfinance segment, a smaller but fast-growing corner of household lending, illustrating that even a moderate aggregate household debt figure can mask real stress concentrated in specific, faster-growing pockets.
Corporate Debt-to-GDP: Deleveraged Since the Mid-2010s Peak

Indian corporate leverage peaked in the mid-2010s, the direct backdrop to the bank NPA crisis Lesson 2 covers in full, when a wave of debt-funded capacity expansion, much of it in infrastructure, power, and metals, ran ahead of the cash flows needed to service it. Since then, many large Indian corporates have genuinely deleveraged, through equity capital raises, asset sales, and a more cautious approach to fresh borrowing, while banks worked through IBC resolutions covered in Chapter 3's Lesson 2. Corporate debt-to-GDP today sits well below its mid-2010s peak, a meaningfully different starting position than an economy still carrying the leverage that caused its last credit event.

Fiscal consolidation and nominal GDP growth outpacing borrowing costs
Rising, from ~30% under a decade ago

children.text: Why This Matters: India Is Not Where the US or Japan Was at Their Cycle Peaks

body.title: India vs a Mature Long-Term Debt Cycle

columns.label: Signature of a Mature Cycle (US, Japan)
points: Government and/or private debt-to-GDP at multi-decade highs
Central bank already at or near the zero lower bound, MP2 or MP3 in use
Ageing, shrinking, or stagnant workforce capping productivity-driven growth
Growth increasingly reliant on asset price gains rather than income growth

columns.label: India's Current Position
points: Combined debt-to-GDP moderate, well below developed-market peaks, and mostly local-currency, domestically held
RBI retains real conventional room; MP1 remains the primary tool
A still-growing, comparatively young workforce, the opposite of Japan's demographic drag from Chapter 4's Lesson 4
Growth still substantially driven by productivity gains, infrastructure buildout, and formalisation, Chapter 1's Force One

body.text: A moderate aggregate picture is not the same as no risk anywhere in the system. Unsecured household credit is growing faster than any other segment covered in this lesson, microfinance asset quality has shown genuine recent stress, and a rapid, broad-based credit expansion from a low base can itself be an early input into a future bubble, exactly the mechanism Chapter 2 built. Reading India's position correctly means holding both facts at once: the aggregate is not late-cycle by global standards, and specific fast-growing pockets deserve the same scrutiny this course has applied to every other credit cycle.

body.title: Pull India's Current Numbers Yourself
steps: Check the RBI's latest Financial Stability Report for current government, household, and corporate debt-to-GDP figures, since the approximate figures in this lesson will have moved by the time you read it
Look up the RBI's most recent data on unsecured retail credit growth and compare it to overall bank credit growth over the same period
Check whether the RBI has taken any further regulatory action, similar to the November 2023 risk-weight change, aimed specifically at unsecured lending or microfinance
Note India's current government debt-to-GDP trend and compare it to the near-90% pandemic peak cited in this lesson

body.title: One Aggregate, Two Reads
body.scenario: A colleague argues: "India's household debt-to-GDP is only around 40%, far below the US or UK, so household credit risk in India is not worth worrying about." You know that unsecured personal loan and credit card growth has run well ahead of overall credit growth for several years, and that microfinance asset quality has recently deteriorated.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's framework, what is your colleague's argument missing, and how would you respond?
body.modelAnswer: Your colleague is reading the aggregate level in isolation, ignoring both the pace of change and the composition within that aggregate, exactly the two things this lesson emphasises alongside the headline number. A 40% household debt-to-GDP ratio is genuinely low by international standards, which is a fair point on its own, but the rapid growth of unsecured lending specifically, well ahead of overall credit growth, is precisely the kind of pattern Chapter 2's bubble checklist flags as worth watching regardless of how low the aggregate starts from. The recent deterioration in microfinance asset quality is a concrete, current example of stress emerging in a fast-growing segment before it necessarily shows up in the aggregate household debt figure at all. The right response is not to dismiss the low aggregate number, but to point out that it coexists with genuine, segment-specific risk that the aggregate number alone cannot reveal, which is exactly why the RBI itself acted on unsecured credit risk weights in November 2023 rather than waiting for the aggregate figure to become alarming.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Which of India's three main debt stocks covered in this lesson is currently growing the fastest, and what regulatory action has the RBI already taken in response?
options: Government debt; the RBI has capped government bond issuance
Corporate debt; the RBI has restricted bank lending to large corporates
Household debt, specifically unsecured retail lending; the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit exposures in November 2023
All three debt stocks are growing at approximately the same rate
body.explanation: Household debt, and unsecured retail lending in particular, has grown faster than government or corporate debt in recent years, prompting the RBI to raise risk weights on unsecured consumer credit exposures for banks and NBFCs in November 2023, a direct regulatory response aimed at slowing that specific segment's growth before it became a larger systemic concern.

body.text: This lesson presents a general educational analysis of India's debt position for teaching purposes and is not investment advice or a market forecast. All debt-to-GDP figures cited are approximate, compiled from RBI, IMF, and Finance Ministry data available up to early 2025, and change with each new data release; verify current figures directly from the RBI's Financial Stability Report, the Union Budget documents, and IMF Article IV consultations before relying on them professionally.

points: India's general government debt-to-GDP rose to nearly 90% during the pandemic and has since eased toward the low-to-mid 80s, well below Chapter 4's Japan case and trending down rather than up

Household debt-to-GDP, at roughly 40%, is low by global standards but is the fastest-growing of India's three debt stocks, driven by unsecured retail lending that the RBI moved to slow in November 2023
Corporate debt-to-GDP has fallen well below its mid-2010s peak, the backdrop to the bank NPA crisis Lesson 2 covers in full, following a sustained period of corporate deleveraging
India's combined debt position, still-growing workforce, and continued reliance on productivity-driven growth do not match the mature long-term debt cycle signature seen in the US or Japan

A moderate aggregate does not mean zero risk: unsecured household credit growth and recent microfinance stress are real, current pockets worth watching closely, which Lesson 3 returns to when building a full current read of India's position
